classification.difficultyReason: Select angle relationships and form simple equations involving equal angles or multiples of an unknown.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess unknown angles at a point.
questions.methodNote: Use 90° right angles, 180° straight angles, 360° revolutions and equal vertically opposite angles. Form and simplify equations as demonstrated in Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select angle relationships and form simple equations involving equal angles or multiples of an unknown.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate nonconcurrent and nonparallel into three pairwise intersections at distinct points, then draw an arrangement satisfying both constraints.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses geometric language through an arrangement satisfying nonconcurrency and nonparallelism.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines lines and concurrent lines. Draw three lines with separate pairwise intersections.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a line arrangement satisfying two stated geometric conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine overlapping angles to find their common sector.

questions.mappingNote: Unknown angles at a point is the closest skill for overlapping sectors.
questions.methodNote: Three-letter angle notation and angle measure; subtract adjacent sectors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine overlapping angles to find their common sector.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise equal vertically opposite angles.

questions.mappingNote: Directly assesses an unknown vertically opposite angle.
questions.methodNote: The context defines intersecting lines and angle notation. Vertically opposite angles can be justified by subtracting each from the same straight angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise equal vertically opposite angles.

classification.difficultyReason: The earlier parts establish both angular rates; the hardest step combines them into relative motion and reverses that relationship to find first-occurrence times.

questions.mappingNote: Unknown angles at a point is the closest catalogue skill for this clock-angle investigation.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines revolutions, right angles and straight angles. Parts b–e establish the angular rates used in f–i; part g uses reflection of the clock positions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use simultaneous hand motion and relative angular speed to find exact times.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the specified line-pair constructions and recognise that their three intersections are collinear; no theorem proof or construction strategy is required.

questions.mappingNote: Geometry language and notation is the closest catalogue match for constructing named line intersections and observing collinearity.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines collinear points. The question supplies the construction and explicitly does not request a proof.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct six joining lines, identify their intersections and observe collinearity without proving the theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught auxiliary-parallel method, choose corresponding or alternate angles, and combine transferred angles with supplementary-angle calculations.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses the Example 2 auxiliary-line method, with supplementary angles where needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 supplies parallel-line angle rules. Page 6 Example 2 draws a parallel through a bend and transfers angles. Page 7 supplies the converse rules.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an auxiliary parallel and combine transferred angles with straight-line angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive suitable angles using triangle or straight-angle sums, then select and justify the converse parallel-line rule establishing the required parallelism.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is establishing parallelism by equal corresponding angles or supplementary co-interior angles, rather than measuring angles.
questions.methodNote: Use transversal angle properties and their converses, with straight-angle calculations. The triangle angle-sum theorem visible on page 9 supports part (c).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove parallelism using converse angle properties, including preliminary angle calculations.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies the explicitly requested theorem, including equations with angle multiples.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies Theorem 3 and Example 2; a adds known angles, b subtracts a known angle, and c–d solve equations containing theta.
questions.methodNote: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies the explicitly requested theorem, including equations with angle multiples.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the equal sides are unspecified and systematically consider all three equal-angle pairings to obtain every possible value.

questions.mappingNote: The equal sides are unspecified, so each possible equal-angle pair must be considered.
questions.methodNote: Equal base angles of an isosceles triangle and the interior-angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires considering all three possible placements of the equal angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove a general result using the triangle angle sum and a right angle.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly proves a consequence of the triangle angle sum.
questions.methodNote: Use the interior-angle sum theorem and the definition of a right-angled triangle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove a general result using the triangle angle sum and a right angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute an angle relationship into the triangle angle sum.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed method matches the angle-sum equations in Example 1.
questions.methodNote: Form an equation using the triangle angle sum, substitute the given relationship and solve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute an angle relationship into the triangle angle sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine a three-part ratio with the triangle angle sum.

questions.mappingNote: The triangle angle sum is the directly assessed geometric fact; ratio notation supplies the angle expressions.
questions.methodNote: Express related angles using one variable, apply the triangle angle sum and solve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine a three-part ratio with the triangle angle sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare angle sums in two nested triangles using a common angle and the given equality.

questions.mappingNote: The proof uses the interior-angle theorem rather than a parallel-line or congruence argument.
questions.methodNote: Use the triangle angle sum in each triangle, retaining the common angle at C and substituting the given equality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare angle sums in two nested triangles using a common angle and the given equality.

classification.difficultyReason: Reframe six unknown shaded angles as three straight angles minus the inner triangle's angle sum, avoiding attempts to calculate individual angles.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 subtracts an inner triangle's angles from three straight angles. Question 9 subtracts the three central angles from three triangle sums.
questions.methodNote: Use the triangle interior-angle sum, straight angles and vertically opposite angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines triangle angle sums with straight-line and vertically opposite angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Use vertically opposite angles to establish the combined central-angle sum, then subtract it from the total angle sums of three triangles.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 subtracts an inner triangle's angles from three straight angles. Question 9 subtracts the three central angles from three triangle sums.
questions.methodNote: Use the triangle interior-angle sum, straight angles and vertically opposite angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines triangle angle sums with straight-line and vertically opposite angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a general inequality proof by comparing the split angles at A and C and explaining why subtracting their smaller sum produces a larger opposite angle.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is proving a geometric inequality; the triangle angle sum supplies the proof.
questions.methodNote: Apply the interior-angle sum to both triangles and compare the split angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires an angle inequality proof using an interior point and two triangle angle sums.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise equal radii as equal sides of triangle ABD, transfer the original triangle's angle at A, and apply isosceles base-angle reasoning.

questions.mappingNote: Assesses combined triangle properties rather than a circle angle theorem.
questions.methodNote: Use triangle angle sums and equal base angles in an isosceles triangle; equal radii identify the isosceles triangle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognises equal radii, then combines right-triangle and isosceles-triangle angle properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Introduce symbolic base angles for both isosceles triangles and combine their triangle sums with the reflex angle's complement around B to prove a general doubling relationship.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is a proof of a property of joined isosceles triangles.
questions.methodNote: Use equal base angles of isosceles triangles, the triangle angle sum and angles at a point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves a relationship between a reflex angle and a composite angle using two isosceles triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Track symbolic angles through two isosceles triangles and their supplementary shared-base angles, then rearrange the resulting relationship for alpha.

questions.mappingNote: Both original questions ask for symbolic formulas using linked triangle properties.
questions.methodNote: Use equal base angles of isosceles triangles, straight angles and the exterior angle theorem.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derives symbolic angle formulas from linked isosceles triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Transfer equal base angles between the two isosceles triangles using an exterior angle, then relate the resulting doubled angle to beta on a straight line.

questions.mappingNote: Both original questions ask for symbolic formulas using linked triangle properties.
questions.methodNote: Use equal base angles of isosceles triangles, straight angles and the exterior angle theorem.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derives symbolic angle formulas from linked isosceles triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines two isosceles triangles and an exterior angle to prove a right angle.

questions.mappingNote: The equal linkage lengths create two isosceles triangles; the exterior angle at M connects their base angles.
questions.methodNote: Triangle interior-angle sum, exterior angle theorem and equal base angles of isosceles triangles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines two isosceles triangles and an exterior angle to prove a right angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Relates base angles of two overlapping isosceles triangles inside a right triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Each side equality gives an isosceles triangle. Their base angles overlap precisely in the labelled angle DBE.
questions.methodNote: Equal base angles in isosceles triangles and the triangle interior-angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Relates base angles of two overlapping isosceles triangles inside a right triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Constructs an equilateral-triangle benchmark using only a compass and explains the angle comparison.

questions.mappingNote: Equal-radius compass arcs construct the equilateral triangle needed for a 60-degree benchmark.
questions.methodNote: An equilateral triangle has three equal 60-degree angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs an equilateral-triangle benchmark using only a compass and explains the angle comparison.

classification.difficultyReason: Use folding invariants to derive a smaller triangle's symbolic integer side lengths, then connect its preserved shape and smaller size to the supplied minimality assumption to obtain a contradiction.

questions.mappingNote: Proof by contradiction is the most advanced directly assessed skill; triangle angle sums and isosceles properties support the construction.
questions.methodNote: Use triangle angle sums and equal base angles of an isosceles triangle. The question supplies folding and the smallest-triangle assumption, which lead to descent and contradiction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses folding to construct a smaller integer-sided triangle and contradict minimality.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a quadrilateral with a reflex interior angle.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill concerns polygon classification; constructing the requested polygon also uses angle classification.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a non-convex polygon: at least one interior angle is reflex.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a quadrilateral with a reflex interior angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Design a simple five-sided polygon with two consecutive inward vertices while checking both interior angles are reflex and the boundary remains valid.

questions.mappingNote: The requested construction combines polygon classification with adjacent reflex-angle identification.
questions.methodNote: Use the five-side definition of a pentagon and the reflex-angle criterion for non-convexity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct five sides with two consecutive reflex vertices.

classification.difficultyReason: Arrange two inward vertices separated by another vertex while retaining a closed, noncrossing five-sided boundary and two reflex interior angles.

questions.mappingNote: The requested construction combines polygon classification with non-adjacent reflex-angle identification.
questions.methodNote: Use the five-side definition of a pentagon and identify reflex interior angles at inward vertices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct five sides with two separated reflex vertices.

classification.difficultyReason: Constructs examples showing that equal angles or equal sides alone do not make a polygon regular.

questions.mappingNote: Both drawing tasks assess the distinction between regular polygons and polygons satisfying only one regularity condition.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 defines a regular polygon as having both equal side lengths and equal interior angles. Its convex and non-convex definitions support the second construction. The polygon angle-sum theorem supports the 120-degree angles in the first construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs examples showing that equal angles or equal sides alone do not make a polygon regular.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish interior from exterior angles, express repeated interior angles as supplements of theta, and solve a routine quadrilateral angle-sum equation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c directly use the quadrilateral sum; b, d and e combine supplementary angles with polygon sums; f directly applies the exterior-angle sum.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 Example 1 uses the quadrilateral interior-angle sum and a linear equation. Page 16 establishes the exterior-angle sum using supplementary interior/exterior pairs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines interior and exterior angle relationships, including linear equations with repeated unknowns.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of sixteen sides into the equal exterior-angle formula.

questions.mappingNote: Directly assesses the exterior angle of a regular polygon.
questions.methodNote: Equal exterior angles of a regular polygon sum to 360 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of sixteen sides into the equal exterior-angle formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Set the polygon interior-angle formula equal to the supplied total and reverse its multiplication and subtraction to find the side count.

questions.mappingNote: Requires reversing the interior-angle sum formula.
questions.methodNote: Use the interior-angle sum (n − 2) × 180 degrees and solve for n.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverses the interior-angle sum formula to determine the number of sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Connects equal interior angles to supplementary exterior angles and determines the side count.

questions.mappingNote: Finds the side count from equal interior angles; equal side lengths are not needed.
questions.methodNote: Interior and exterior angles are supplementary; equal exterior angles sum to 360 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connects equal interior angles to supplementary exterior angles and determines the side count.

classification.difficultyReason: Divides the exterior-angle sum by the given equal exterior angle.

questions.mappingNote: The catalogue's regular-polygon exterior-angle skill is the closest match; the calculation needs only equal exterior angles.
questions.methodNote: Divide the 360-degree exterior-angle sum by each equal exterior angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divides the exterior-angle sum by the given equal exterior angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the side count into the interior-angle sum formula, then use regularity to divide that supplied intermediate result equally among the angles.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the sum formula; part b directly assesses the regular-polygon interior angle.
questions.methodNote: Use (n−2)×180° for the interior-angle sum, then divide by n for a regular polygon.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into the interior-angle formulas.

classification.difficultyReason: Extends the formula to a divisibility condition and enumerates every possible side count.

questions.mappingNote: Part a evaluates the formula for eight side counts; part b extends that same formula to all eligible integers n.
questions.methodNote: Apply the regular-polygon interior-angle formula; rewrite it as 180−360/n to identify the integer-angle condition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extends the formula to a divisibility condition and enumerates every possible side count.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer two isosceles triangles from equal square and equilateral sides, then link their base angles to the square corners and the target triangle.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded equilateral triangle creates two isosceles triangles; geometrical angle reasoning is the directly assessed method.
questions.methodNote: Use equal base angles in isosceles triangles, the 60° angles of an equilateral triangle, square right angles and triangle angle sums.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines square, equilateral-triangle and isosceles-triangle angle properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses the angle sum with proportional unknown angles.

questions.mappingNote: The same quadrilateral angle-sum method applies to the four ratio terms.
questions.methodNote: Example 1(b) sums proportional unknown angles to 360 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses the angle sum with proportional unknown angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Group the eight marked sectors into four straight-angle complements and subtract the inner quadrilateral's total rather than seeking individual angle measures.

questions.mappingNote: The eight marked sectors are obtained by subtracting the inner quadrilateral's angles from four straight angles.
questions.methodNote: Polygon interior-angle sums and pairing interior and exterior angles on a straight line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines four straight angles with the inner quadrilateral angle sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Derives a general counting formula and accounts for double counting.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is a general combinatorial count of diagonals; the supplied catalogue has no dedicated polygon-diagonal skill.
questions.methodNote: Polygon vertices and sides are defined in the teaching; the diagonal definition is supplied in the question. Count eligible endpoint pairs and remove double counting.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derives a general counting formula and accounts for double counting.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines regular-polygon and isosceles-triangle angles to prove parallelism.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied teacher proof assumes a regular pentagon; this necessary given is added explicitly.
questions.methodNote: Use the regular-polygon interior-angle formula, equal base angles in an isosceles triangle, and the converse of the co-interior angle property.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines regular-polygon and isosceles-triangle angles to prove parallelism.

classification.difficultyReason: Move from a regular numerical case to an arbitrary star, recognise exterior angles counted twice across the tip triangles, and generalise that counting argument to n tips.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) uses regular-pentagon angles to find a tip; part (b) sums the five tip triangles without regularity; part (c) generalises the same polygon-angle reasoning. The general polygon angle-sum skill is the closest existing catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 establishes polygon interior-angle sums and regular interior angles; page 16 establishes the exterior-angle sum. Combine those results with triangle angle sums and supplementary angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises polygon and triangle angle sums to stars without assuming regularity.

classification.difficultyReason: Invent a quadrilateral assembled from three equilateral triangles and verify that three congruent copies can be rearranged into a larger equilateral triangle, with neither dissection supplied.

questions.mappingNote: Geometric shape reasoning is the closest available skill for this dissection riddle.
questions.methodNote: Use polygon composition and the equal sides and angles of equilateral triangles. The teacher answer supplies the dissection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infers a quadrilateral from two geometric dissection constraints.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses an embedded definition to identify face–vertex relationships between all five Platonic solids.

questions.mappingNote: Geometry language and notation is the closest supplied catalogue skill; no supplied skill specifically assesses polyhedral duality.
questions.methodNote: Use the five Platonic solids and the definition of duality embedded in the question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses an embedded definition to identify face–vertex relationships between all five Platonic solids.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires a general geometric construction showing that every triangle tiles the plane.

questions.mappingNote: Proof of triangle and quadrilateral properties is the closest supplied skill for the general triangle-to-parallelogram construction.
questions.methodNote: Use the embedded tessellation definition; pair half-turned triangles into parallelograms, then repeat in rows as in the matched teacher solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a general geometric construction showing that every triangle tiles the plane.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires translating tessellation into an integer number of equal angles around a vertex, bounding the possible counts and identifying which yield integer polygon side counts.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses which regular polygons can meet edge-to-edge without gaps, using interior angles and integer numbers of polygons at a vertex.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 states the regular-polygon interior-angle formula; page 16 demonstrates substitution into it; page 17 considers regular polygons meeting at a vertex. Combine this angle formula with a full turn of 360 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines regular-polygon angles with integer constraints to determine every possible edge-to-edge tessellation.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires inventing matching-boundary constructions beyond regular polygons and a general side-count argument covering every integer, with no construction scaffold supplied.

questions.mappingNote: General geometrical reasoning is the closest catalogue skill; restricting the task to regular polygons would change its answer.
questions.methodNote: Use polygon definitions and arrangements of copies around vertices; non-convex polygons are allowed. The teacher solution supplies the matching-boundary construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires examples and a construction covering arbitrarily many polygon sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires expressing the angle sequence sum using an unknown number of sides, solving the resulting quadratic and using convexity to reject an otherwise valid algebraic root.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is the polygon interior-angle sum; the sequence supplies the individual angles.
questions.methodNote: Apply the interior-angle sum (n−2)×180° and the definition that every interior angle of a convex polygon is less than 180°.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Equates an arithmetic sum to the polygon angle sum, solves a quadratic and rejects a root using convexity.

classification.difficultyReason: The hint supplies planar reduction, but the student must devise triangulation and boundary-removal steps, prove their count changes preserve the characteristic and connect the terminal triangle to the original solid.

questions.mappingNote: No supplied catalogue entry directly covers Euler's formula; proof terminology is the closest general proof skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the polyhedron and convexity definitions, the question's face-removal/projection hint, and the supplied teacher method of triangulation and invariant boundary removal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a general invariant proof through planar projection, triangulation and boundary removal.

classification.difficultyReason: The parts scaffold face, edge and vertex counting and Euler substitution, but finding H additionally requires extracting the one-pentagon/two-hexagon vertex pattern from the image and forming a new incidence relation.

questions.mappingNote: The provided catalogue has no Euler-formula or polyhedral-incidence skill. angle-properties-plane-shapes is the closest available geometrical-reasoning classification.
questions.methodNote: Pages 14–16 establish polygon terminology and polygon angle sums. Page 17 introduces polyhedrons and the number of faces meeting at vertices. Question 30 on page 20 supplies the Euler-characteristic result used here. Count faces, double-count shared edges and triple-count vertices before applying Euler's formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires incidence counting, algebraic cancellation and Euler's formula to determine the numbers of polygonal faces.
